summary: Proxy Mobile IPv6 sends all traffic through a local mobility anchor, which may be inefficient. Localized Routing lets mobile nodes on the same or different access gateways exchange traffic more directly.

eli5.summary: Two neighbors would not mail letters through a far-away post office if they could hand them over the fence.

questions: what is localized routing in pmipv6
how to avoid the lma for local traffic
what is the difference between lri and lra
what is scenario a21 in pmipv6
subtitle: Let two mobile nodes in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain talk directly instead of detouring through the anchor.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 sends all traffic through the local mobility anchor. When both endpoints are in the same domain, that adds delay, congestion, transport cost and load at the anchor.
tldr.mechanism: Two new Mobility Header messages, Localized Routing Initiation (LRI) and Localized Routing Acknowledgment (LRA), let the anchor (or in one case the gateway) tell the gateways to forward traffic locally or through a direct tunnel between them.
tldr.outcome: Localized routing works for three of the four anchor and gateway layouts. The fourth, different gateways and different anchors, is not covered. The state is temporary and falls back to the anchor path.

today: RFC 6705 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5213 and the problem statement in RFC 6279.

sections.title: Why Localize the Path
sections.content:
In Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213), a mobile access gateway (MAG) signals for each attached mobile node (MN), and a local mobility anchor (LMA) holds a bidirectional tunnel to each MAG for all of the nodes' data traffic. If both endpoints are in the same domain, sending their traffic via the LMA can be suboptimal. The RFC lists increased delay and congestion, higher transport costs and more traffic load at the LMA.

Localized routing (LR) lets nodes on the same or different MAGs exchange traffic directly, using local forwarding or a direct tunnel between the gateways. The problem statement is in RFC 6279. This document assumes each MN is attached to a MAG that has already set up a binding at its LMA.
sections.eli5: Walking a letter all the way to the central post office and back, just to reach the house next door, wastes time. This RFC lets the neighbors skip the trip.

sections.title: Who Starts Localized Routing and How It Ends
sections.content:
To avoid ambiguity, the RFC fixes the initiator. The MAG MUST initiate LR if both nodes are attached to it but anchored at different LMAs, and MUST NOT initiate it otherwise. The LMA MUST initiate LR if both nodes are anchored to it, and MUST NOT otherwise.

LR is not persistent. It has a lifetime set by the initiator, and on expiry forwarding MUST revert to the bidirectional tunnel and the Localized Routing Entries (LREs) MUST be removed. To stop early, the initiator sends a new LRI with the lifetime set to zero. How traffic that deserves LR is detected is left open. One example given is an application-layer signaling entity notifying the LMA.
sections.eli5: The rule says who gets to shout 'let us use the shortcut' so two people do not both do it. The shortcut also times out on its own, like a parking ticket.

sections.title: The Supported Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC names scenarios by how many MAGs and LMAs are involved. In A11 (same MAG, same LMA), the LMA sends an LRI to the MAG with the MN-ID and Home Network Prefix (HNP) of both nodes. The MAG checks its binding cache and that EnableMAGLocalRouting is 1, otherwise it rejects with an LRA carrying status Localized Routing Not Allowed. If allowed, it creates LREs that override the Binding Update List entries for those HNPs, so matching traffic is forwarded locally. If delivery through the LREs fails, the MAG MUST fall back to the BUL entry.

In A21 (different MAGs, same LMA), the LMA MUST send two separate LRIs, each also carrying the counterpart MAG's IPv6 address, and each MAG forwards through a tunnel to the other. No synchronization between MAGs is needed. If only one MAG accepts, one direction is local and the other still goes through the LMA.

In A12 (same MAG, different LMAs), neither LMA can tell the nodes share a MAG, so the MAG sends an LRI to each LMA. Each LMA decides on its own policy, and the MAG concludes it can forward locally only after both return status zero.

A22 (different MAGs and different LMAs) is not covered, because PMIPv6 has no inter-LMA communication. If A12 turns into A22, the initiator MUST tear LR down, which can cause transient packet loss. Where that is possible, LR is NOT RECOMMENDED for loss-sensitive applications.
sections.eli5: It depends who lives where. If both friends use the same mail room and the same building, the manager says 'hand it over'. If they live in different buildings, each building gets a note about the other.

sections.title: Handover and Tunnels Between Gateways
sections.content:
When a node moves to a new MAG, LR state must be re-established. The LMA, on receiving the PBU from the new MAG, sees LR is active for that node and MUST initiate LR at the new MAG and update the old one. In A21 it also updates the other MAG to point at the new one. In A12 the old MAG MUST immediately stop using the LRE and send the other node's packets to its LMA.

For the tunnel between two MAGs, both SHOULD support the same encapsulations as the LMA-MAG tunnel: IPv4-or-IPv6-over-IPv6, over-IPv4, over-IPv4-UDP, TLV-header UDP, and GRE with or without keys. Both MUST use the same mechanism. By default, the inter-MAG tunnel uses whatever the LMA-MAG tunnel uses. It can be overridden by configuration, which must match on both MAGs, or by a negotiation mechanism that is out of scope.

IPv4 home addresses are supported by adding them to the LREs, including an IPv4 HoA option in the messages, and encapsulating LRI and LRA like PBU and PBA when the transport network is IPv4-only.
sections.eli5: If a friend moves to a new street, the manager tells both sides the new address. The two neighbors must also agree to wrap their packages the same way.

sections.title: LRI, LRA and the MAG Address Option
sections.content:
LRI uses Mobility Header type 17 and LRA uses type 18. The LRI carries a Sequence Number, a Lifetime in seconds (0xffff means infinite, 0 means stop) and mobility options. The options MUST hold two MN-ID options, each followed by one or more HNPs, in the order [MN1-ID, MN1-HNP], [MN2-ID, MN2-HNP], and MAY include the remote MAG IPv6 address option. An unanswered LRI SHOULD be retransmitted.

The LRA copies the Sequence Number and has a U flag (1 means unsolicited), an 8-bit Status, and a Lifetime. Status values below 128 mean success. Defined values are 0 Success, 128 Localized Routing Not Allowed and 129 MN Not Attached. On status 0 the options repeat the tuples from the LRI. Otherwise they list only those for which local forwarding is supported.

The new MAG IPv6 Address option has type 51, Length 18 and Address Length 128, followed by a 16-byte address.
sections.eli5: The request is a form listing the two people and how long the shortcut should last. The reply is the same form stamped yes or no, with a reason if no.

sections.title: Configuration, Security and IANA
sections.content:
Two variables must be configurable: LRA_WAIT_TIME (default 3 seconds between LRI retransmissions) and LRI_RETRIES (default 3).

The protocol inherits the threats in RFC 4832 and uses the LMA-MAG security association from RFC 5213 to protect LRI and LRA. It assumes a MAG-MAG security association exists where LR runs between MAGs. Integrity protection using IPsec is REQUIRED, confidentiality OPTIONAL. MAGs MUST do ingress filtering on MN-sourced packets before putting them in MAG-MAG tunnels to prevent address spoofing.

IANA assigned Mobility Header types 17 and 18 and Mobility Option type 51.
sections.eli5: The messages must be sealed so nobody can fake them, and each gateway checks who a packet really came from before sending it down the shortcut.
